content.text: In C#, implement a checkout-price calculator for one caller-supplied item price. The item price, discount rate, and tax rate are exact decimal strings in plain nonnegative decimal notation: digits with an optional decimal point, and no sign, exponent, whitespace, or separator. Discount and tax rates must be in the inclusive range [0, 1] and are decimal fractions, so "0.1" means 10%. Return the final total as an exact decimal string with exactly two decimal places, rounded using half-even rounding. The caller selects standard or expedited shipping. Apply the discount only to the item price. If expedited shipping is used, add a 15.00 fee after that discount and before tax.

item.text: I’ll inspect the existing C# project and add the calculator with exact-decimal handling and focused tests.

The project is a single stub, so I’m making the public surface explicit: `Calculate(itemPrice, discountRate, taxRate, expeditedShipping)` plus a `ShippingMethod` overload. Internally it will use arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic rather than `decimal`, so long valid inputs remain exact.

item.text: The implementation now validates the strict input grammar and computes discount, shipping, and tax as one rational value before cent rounding. I’m doing a final source-level check; this workspace has no .NET compiler or project file to run locally.

Implemented the checkout calculator in [CheckoutPriceCalculator.cs](/home/gili/cat/worktrees/v1.0/.cat/temp/changelog-language-captures/csharp-code-codex-base.bM62oG/codex/mss80bpo-zffbsj5tc/project/CheckoutPriceCalculator.cs).

It provides `Calculate` overloads using either a `bool` or `ShippingMethod`, validates strict decimal input and rate bounds, applies shipping/tax in the required order, and formats half-even rounded totals to exactly two decimals. It uses `BigInteger` arithmetic for exact results beyond `decimal` precision.

No .NET compiler or project file is present in the workspace, so I could not run a build locally.
